Rigetti secures $100m under the CHIPS Act
Rigetti Computing has reached a definitive agreement with the US Department of Commerce for $100m in funding. Granted under the CHIPS Act, the package is intended to support the group's research and development work in superconducting quantum computing. In return, Washington will receive a minority, non-controlling stake in Rigetti.
RIGETTI COMPUTING, INC.
The funding will allow the company to pursue three R&D projects aimed at clearing several technical hurdles to scaling superconducting quantum systems. Rigetti aims to accelerate its roadmap toward systems capable of supporting real-world applications at scale. The announcement was well received on the stock market, with the shares up more than 7.8% at the opening of Wall Street on Tuesday.

pages.title: Rigetti (RGTI) Stock Prediction: $40 Bull, $9 Bear
pages.text:
Rigetti (RGTI) Stock Prediction: $40 Bull Case, $9 Bear Case
The popular story about Rigetti Computing is that Wall Street has turned on the quantum computing trade. It has not. Pull the analyst sheet and something stranger shows up: across the 13 analysts covering RGTI, the lowest twelve-month price target on the tape is $17.30, and the stock closed at $15.95 on 28 September 2026. Not one published target sits below the market price. The sell side does not have a bear case for Rigetti — it has a spread of bull cases of differing enthusiasm. That matters more than any single number, because it means the $5.32bn market capitalisation is being defended by a research community that has no modelled downside, on a company that booked $13.35m of revenue over the trailing twelve months. That is roughly 398 times sales. The stock is down 71.7% from its 52-week high and the consensus target still implies 79% upside.
Here is the part no one writes down. If you strip out the balance sheet, the valuation stops looking like a technology multiple and starts looking like a clinical-stage biotech. Rigetti finished Q2 FY2026 with $541.3m in cash, cash equivalents and available-for-sale investments. Against a $5.32bn market cap, that cash is about 10% of the price. The other 90% — call it $4.8bn — is a pure option on a physics result that has not happened yet. Biotech investors have a vocabulary for this. They do not value a phase-two oncology company on a revenue multiple; they value it on the probability-weighted outcome of one trial, and they know the readout date. Quantum hardware is being traded the same way, except most equity investors are still reaching for price-to-sales, a ratio that tells you nothing useful at 398 times. The readout for Rigetti is not a trial. It is a number called coherence time, and management has told you exactly where it sits.
RGTI closed at $15.95 on 28 September 2026, down 46.2% over twelve months and 71.7% below its 52-week high of $56.34 — Nasdaq daily closes, retrieved 29 September 2026
Market capitalisation $5.32bn on trailing-twelve-month revenue of $13.35m, a price-to-sales multiple of roughly 398x — StockAnalysis, 29 September 2026
Q2 FY2026 revenue $5.1m, operating loss $28.1m, cash and investments $541.3m — Rigetti Q2 2026 results, 6 August 2026
Consensus target $28.53 across 13 analysts; street high $40, street low $17.30 — every published target is above the spot price — StockAnalysis, 29 September 2026
Cepheus-1-108Q runs 108 qubits as twelve linked 9-qubit chiplets at 99.1% median two-qubit gate fidelity, against a stated 99.5% target for later in 2026 — The Quantum Insider, April 2026
Coherence time, the binding constraint, sits at 25 to 30 microseconds — Rigetti Q2 FY2026 earnings call
Rigetti signed a $100m definitive agreement with the US Department of Commerce — StockAnalysis company summary, September 2026
What is actually happening, and why the chart looks like this
Rigetti builds superconducting quantum processors — tiny circuits of aluminium and niobium printed on silicon, chilled to a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, where they behave as artificial atoms. The commercial product is access: customers rent time on the machines through Rigetti’s own cloud, and through Amazon Braket, Microsoft Azure Quantum and qBraid. Some buy a system outright. That is a real business, and it is growing — but it is growing from a base so small that a single on-premises sale moves the quarterly line.
The technical story in 2026 has been Cepheus-1-108Q. Rather than fabricate one large chip and accept the yield penalty, Rigetti tiles twelve 9-qubit chiplets and links them, which is why the company describes it as the industry’s largest modular quantum system. Modularity is the right call — it is the same argument that pushed classical semiconductors toward chiplets, and we have covered that shift in the context of Intel’s own packaging roadmap. But modularity solves manufacturing, not physics.
The physics problem is coherence. A qubit holds its quantum state for a finite window before the environment scrambles it, and every gate operation has to fit inside that window. Rigetti’s gates are genuinely fast — roughly 60 nanoseconds for a two-qubit operation, which is among the quickest in superconducting hardware — and single-qubit fidelity is already at 99.9%. Two-qubit fidelity is the one that matters for real algorithms, and it is stuck at 99.1% because coherence times sit at 25 to 30 microseconds. Management was unusually direct about this on the Q2 call, naming coherence as the limiting factor and pointing to a specific fix: capping the niobium with tantalum, a materials change the team believes can deliver a two-to-threefold improvement.
That is the whole investment case compressed into one materials-science bet. “We remain focused on delivering against the milestones we have laid out, including fidelity improvements on Cepheus-1-108Q, higher qubit systems and disciplined execution of our capital plan,” chief executive Subodh Kulkarni told investors alongside the Q2 results. Read that literally: the company is telling you the milestone list is the thesis.
What the analysts and the counterparties are actually doing
The absence of a published bear case is not laziness. It is a structural feature of how small-cap deep-tech coverage works, and it has a cost for anyone using consensus as a guide.
Look at who covers the name. Benchmark’s David Williams has argued the quantum sector is accelerating and that Rigetti’s long-term strategy is supported by its execution. B. Riley Securities’ Craig Ellis raised his target from $19 to $35 while keeping a Buy. Needham has sat at $18 on a Buy. Cantor Fitzgerald initiated at Overweight. These are genuinely different views — a $17-to-$40 band is a factor of 2.4 — but they are all expressions of the same underlying stance, which is that the technology arrives. No one on the sheet is publishing the scenario where it arrives late enough that the cash runs down first.
Meanwhile the counterparties are voting with contracts rather than opinions, and their behaviour is more informative. Amazon, Microsoft and qBraid have all kept Rigetti hardware on their quantum cloud menus — which is a low-cost commitment, since none of them is taking inventory risk. The US Department of Commerce signed a $100m definitive agreement, and the UK has provided support as well. That is the tell worth watching: governments are funding the research, hyperscalers are reselling the access, and neither group is buying the company. Compare that with how compute demand gets financed elsewhere in AI, where counterparties take real balance-sheet exposure — Anthropic committed $11.6bn to Akamai and took a warrant struck at $111.33. Nobody is writing that kind of paper on quantum hardware yet.
The peer set tells the same story. IonQ has pushed its first Superion-256 revenue recognition out to late 2027, which is the sector’s honest admission that commercial quantum is a 2027-and-beyond revenue event, not a 2026 one. Rigetti’s own $13.35m of trailing revenue says the same thing in a different notation.
The market impact: what 398 times sales is actually pricing
Run the arithmetic in both directions, because it is more revealing than the multiple itself.
At $15.95 and 333.77m shares outstanding, Rigetti is a $5.32bn company. Net of $541.3m in cash and investments, the operating business is being valued at roughly $4.8bn. Trailing revenue is $13.35m and the trailing net loss is $238.67m. For the enterprise value to compress to a merely expensive 50 times sales — the kind of multiple a fast-growing infrastructure software company might carry — revenue would need to reach about $96m. That is a 7.2x increase from here.
Now the other direction. Q2 burned $28.1m at the operating line. Against $541.3m of cash, that is roughly nineteen quarters of runway at the current rate — call it four and a half years, before any capital raise and before the burn rate rises as headcount and fabrication scale. Rigetti is not, on this evidence, a solvency story in the near term. It is a duration story: the company can afford to wait, and the question is whether shareholders can afford to wait at this price.
Tantalum capping lifts coherence 2–3x and two-qubit fidelity clears 99.5% on schedule Coherence improvement lands late or partially; the 99.5% target slips into 2027
$541.3m cash funds the roadmap without dilution through 2029 Burn rises with fabrication scale and a raise arrives at a depressed price
Government contracts convert into recurring, budgeted programme revenue Government money stays project-shaped and never compounds into a run-rate
Modular chiplets prove out and qubit count scales without a fidelity penalty Chiplet interconnects add error faster than the materials fix removes it
Quantum sentiment re-rates the whole sector as it did in late 2025 Sentiment normalises toward the peer group and the multiple compresses
The bear column produces $9 in a specific way, and it is worth being explicit rather than hand-waving. At $9, Rigetti is a $3.0bn company — still about 225 times trailing sales, still 5.5 times its own cash pile, and still comfortably the second-largest listed pure-play in superconducting quantum. In other words, $9 is not a distress price. It is what the stock looks like if the technology stays on track but the market stops paying a scarcity premium for it, which is roughly what happened to the name between October 2025 and March 2026 when it fell from $56.34 to $12.90. The bear case here is a sentiment case, not a bankruptcy case. Anyone modelling actual failure would need a number well below $9, and that scenario is not what the $12.90 low tested.
Policy is the swing factor, and it cuts both ways
Quantum computing sits in an unusual policy position: it is simultaneously a subsidised national-security priority and a future regulatory target, and Rigetti is exposed to both.
On the subsidy side, the $100m Department of Commerce agreement is the most concrete validation Rigetti has. Washington has decided that domestic quantum fabrication is strategic, in much the same way it decided domestic leading-edge logic was strategic. That is a genuine tailwind, and it is the reason the cash position looks as comfortable as it does. The UK has provided support too, which diversifies the political risk.
The tension is that government money is not commercial revenue, and investors frequently conflate the two. A programme contract is milestone-shaped: it funds specific deliverables over a defined period, it does not renew automatically, and it produces lumpy recognition rather than a compounding run rate. When Rigetti reports a strong quarter driven by a Novera QPU sale to a government lab, that is a real sale — but it is not the same signal as a commercial customer expanding cloud consumption for the fourth quarter running. The market has not consistently distinguished between the two, and the day it starts to is the day the multiple gets tested.
The second policy vector is export control. Quantum processors with credible cryptanalytic potential are exactly the class of technology that attracts controls, and the direction of travel in Washington has been toward more restriction, not less. For Rigetti that is double-edged: controls entrench domestic players against Chinese competition, but they also fence off addressable market and add compliance cost to a company with 333.77m shares and $13.35m of revenue. A third vector, further out, is the “harvest now, decrypt later” problem driving post-quantum cryptography migration deadlines across financial infrastructure. That is a demand tailwind for the sector, but it accrues to whoever has a working machine when the deadlines bite — which returns the argument, again, to coherence time.
Three things are worth watching, in order of how much they move the price.
First, the fidelity print. Rigetti has committed to

IonQ vs. Rigetti: Is the Quantum Rally Backed by Fundamentals, or Just Momentum?
IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ) jumped roughly 12% in premarket trading on September 23 after testing the industry's first real-time quantum error decoder, then extended gains on reveals that its Superion quantum processor would be integrated into NVIDIA's Accelerated Quantum Research Center with Rigetti Computing, Inc. (NASDAQ:RGTI) trading up in sympathy on the same announcement, as the two stocks typically move together on sector-validating news. That said, a shared rally obscures a valuation gap between the two that's far wider than most sector-wide coverage lets on.
Curious to see how far Wall Street thinks the rally will go? BofA recently put a $60 price target on IonQ, here's the bull case in full.
IonQ's second-quarter revenue came in at $80 million, up 287% year-over-year, and management boosted its 2026 projection to $280-290 million, with combined revenue (after closing the SkyWater foundry purchase) potentially reaching $460 million for the year. The company had roughly $2 billion in pro-forma cash, cash equivalents and investments following the SkyWater acquisition, dwarfing Rigetti's approximately $540 million, giving IonQ significantly more runway to fund years of pre-commercial R&D without fear of dilution.
On the tech front, IonQ's trapped-ion design appears to have an accuracy advantage in recent comparisons, with IonQ reporting strong two-qubit gate-fidelity results, although direct comparisons with Rigetti are not straightforward. However, Rigetti's architecture offers an advantage in terms of speed. The distinction is significant because quantum computing is not a simple race in which one company is "ahead" on every metric: accuracy, gate speed, scalability, connectivity, and error correction are all important. IonQ's advantage is thus best regarded as a technical and financial one, rather than proof that it has already won the architecture race. Rigetti remains open to the potential that advancements in speed, production, or error correction could close the gap.
The valuation gap gets flattened when these two stocks are discussed together. IonQ's market capitalization is currently around $17.48 billion, compared to combined 2026 revenue guidance of $450 million to $460 million following the SkyWater acquisition, putting its forward price-to-sales multiple in the 39x range. This is already a notable multiple, but it is built on a path to nearly triple-digit revenue growth and a roughly $2 billion of pro-forma cash, cash equivalents and investments that reduces near-term funding risk.
Meanwhile, Rigetti, with a market capitalization that has fluctuated between $5 billion to $9 billion over the last year, trades at an unusual trailing price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 391.65x, having previously reached nearly 1,000x during substantial trading spikes.
While trailing multiples for both businesses remain elevated due to small historical sales bases, the valuation gap remains substantial. Simply put, the market is charging investors much more per dollar of current revenue for Rigetti than for IonQ, despite IonQ having a far stronger balance sheet and a larger revenue base.
That disparity becomes significant because it signals potential downside risk if sentiment cools. A stock trading at 39x forward sales has priced in high growth, while a stock trading at several hundred times trailing sales has priced in near-perfect execution over a much longer time horizon, with far less revenue currently on the books to anchor that multiple if the growth narrative stalls even briefly.
Insider selling adds another cautious signal to the group. Since September 2024, insiders at IonQ, Rigetti, D-Wave, and Quantum Computing Inc. have collectively sold around $895.1 million more stock than they bought. On September 11, IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi sold 16,121 shares for around $598,000, though the filing said that the transaction was non-discretionary and was used to meet tax obligations related to vested restricted stock units.
Hedge fund positioning has grown for both companies, although Rigetti Computing, Inc. (NASDAQ:RGTI) has seen a greater gain. The number of hedge funds owning IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ) jumped from 39 in the first quarter to 42 in the second, while Rigetti's ownership increased from 29 to 34 funds. That suggests that institutional investors are increasing exposure to the quantum theme rather than focusing solely on the better-capitalized leader. The short-interest numbers reflect a far wider contrast over Rigetti: short interest is 10.15% of IonQ's shares versus 19.07% for Rigetti.
Neither stock is a value investment, since both remain speculative bets on a technology that is still years away from widespread commercial application. However, the valuation math argues for treating them very differently within that assumption. IonQ's multiple, while extreme by any conventional measure, is supported by a larger revenue base, faster reported growth, and a cash position that provides years of runway without dilution risk. Rigetti's multiple requires investors to pay several times more per dollar of current sales for a company with a fraction of the cash cushion, implying that any slowdown in its growth rate or the need to raise capital would cause the stock to fall from a far less defensible valuation baseline. Investors drawn to the sector by names like these should treat the price-to-sales gap, not just the shared NVIDIA headline, as the more important number, and should keep an eye on upcoming quarters to see if Rigetti's own revenue growth can actually close that multiple gap, or if the current premium is simply compensation that the market hasn't yet demanded fully.
While we acknowledge the potential of IONQ as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. IonQ vs. Rigetti Computing: Which Pure-Play Quantum Stock Actually Has the Technology Edge?
IonQ still appears to have the accuracy edge, while its connectivity and early progress on error-correction strengthen its advantage.
Rigetti Computing's 108-qubit system is much faster, but its larger systems showed lower accuracy.
The winners of the quantum race will be decided by how well their technologies perform at much larger scales.
IonQ(NYSE: IONQ) and Rigetti Computing(NASDAQ: RGTI) are taking entirely different technological routes in their efforts to build useful quantum computers.
IonQ uses trapped-ion technology, where individual charged atoms held in place by precise electromagnetic fields serve as qubits, the basic units of information in any quantum computer. Rigetti Computing uses superconducting qubits, which are tiny electrical circuits cooled to extremely low temperatures.
Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Image source: Getty Images.
IonQ has demonstrated more than 99.99% fidelity, or accuracy, for 2-qubit gates (operations performed on 2 qubits at the same time). Rigetti Computing has reported roughly 99.1% median 2-qubit fidelity on its 108-qubit Cepheus system. Hence, its typical 2-qubit operation succeeds about 99.1% of the time.
While IonQ may appear to be the obvious technology winner, these figures are not directly comparable. IonQ's 99.99% result came from testing a particular 2-qubit operation, rather than measuring the overall performance of a large commercial quantum computer. A more comparable measure comes from IonQ's Forte systems, which have reported a median 2-qubit fidelity of 99.3% to 99.5%. Hence, although IonQ's qubits still appear to perform operations more accurately than Rigetti Computing's, the gap in accuracy between them is much smaller.
That narrower accuracy gap could prove crucial when quantum calculations become more complex. Using the more comparable figures above, 99.5% fidelity implies an error rate of roughly 0.5%, compared with about 0.9% at 99.1%. Hence, Rigetti Computing's error rate is roughly 1.8 times as high in this comparison.
IonQ also has an advantage in how its qubits communicate. The company's trapped-ion systems offer all-to-all connectivity, meaning any qubit can directly interact with another qubit in the system.
Quantum computers with more limited connectivity may need additional operations, known as SWAP gates, to move quantum information between qubits that cannot directly interact. These extra operations can introduce more errors.
IonQ's connectivity can therefore reduce the number of operations needed for some quantum calculations. This can partly offset IonQ's slower quantum gates, which are the basic operations performed on qubits. In one published comparison, IonQ's Forte systems took about 950 microseconds for a 2-qubit gate, while Rigetti Computing's 108-qubit Cepheus system performed such gates in about 60 nanoseconds.
IonQ also needs to prove that the advantages of trapped-ion technology persist as its quantum computers become larger. The company's next-generation Superion 256 platform is designed around 256 qubits. IonQ has already manufactured 256-qubit Superion processor chips at SkyWater, the semiconductor foundry it acquired in July. The company has also successfully trapped ions on prototype versions of the system. However, these systems are not yet being delivered to customers; commercial deliveries are expected to begin in 2027.
In short, the Superion 256 is an important milestone, but the real test for IonQ will be whether its hardware can maintain high accuracy and connectivity as the number of qubits increases.
IonQ has also made progress in quantum error correction, which combines multiple physical qubits to create more reliable logical qubits. In one experiment, the company used 18 physical qubits to encode 4 logical qubits. Some of those logical qubits preserved quantum information for about as long as, or slightly longer than, the individual physical qubits. Researchers call this breakeven performance. This is still far from a fault-tolerant quantum computer, but it shows that IonQ has begun demonstrating its error-correction approach on actual hardware rather than only through simulations.
DARPA -- the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency -- has also advanced IonQ to Stage B of its Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. At this stage, the agency is evaluating the company's development plan, technical risks, and the prototypes needed to reduce those risks.
Rigetti Computing's quantum computing technology
Rigetti's much faster quantum computing operations could give it a major advantage if it can improve accuracy while building larger systems.
The company has already made progress on the scale front. Its 108-qubit Cepheus system combines 12 interconnected 9-qubit chiplets into a 108-qubit processor. Chiplets are smaller processor blocks that can be connected to build larger systems. Rigetti Computing says this approach can help it increase the qubit counts of its quantum computers while avoiding the manufacturing complexities of building increasingly large chips.
However, Rigetti Computing has reported a median 2-qubit fidelity of 99.8% on its 9-qubit system and 99.6% on its 36-qubit system. The figure fell to roughly 99.1% on the 108-qubit Cepheus system. So while it has demonstrated that it can build larger quantum computers, maintaining accuracy as qubit count increases remains a challenge.
Management has set a goal of developing a system with roughly 1,000 qubits, 99.9% 2-qubit fidelity, and 2-qubit operations that take less than 50 nanoseconds, and given itself a timeline of approximately three years. If Rigetti Computing can build a single quantum computer that achieves all of those milestones, its combination of speed, accuracy, and scale could significantly narrow the gap between its tech and IonQ's.
Which company has the technology edge?
I think IonQ has the technology edge today. The company has moved beyond building more physical qubits to demonstrating error correction on actual hardware.
However, its lead is not secure. The Superion 256 is still in the prototype stage. IonQ still needs to prove that its accuracy and connectivity can hold up as its systems become much larger. Rigetti Computing could narrow the gap if it improves accuracy while preserving its existing advantages in speed and scalability.

Is the future of computing quantum or conversational? Investors deciding between Rigetti Computing (RGTI -0.66%) and SoundHound AI (SOUN +0.69%) must choose which high-growth technology offers the better long-term potential for their portfolios.
Rigetti is a pioneer in building superconducting quantum computers, while SoundHound provides voice-enabled artificial intelligence software for diverse industries. They are being compared because both represent small-cap bets on the next generation of artificial intelligence, though they operate at opposite ends of the hardware and software spectrum.
Rigetti sells superconducting quantum processors and cloud-based quantum services to research and commercial clients. The company remains a pioneer among tech stocks, particularly within the nascent quantum hardware industry. It serves customers through its Quantum Cloud Services platform, targeting complex problems in fields like climate simulation and drug discovery. Major partners include Amazon (AMZN -0.05%) and Microsoft (MSFT +1.48%), which provide broad cloud access to its hardware. Significant government clients like DARPA also utilize its technology, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.
In FY 2025, according to its latest annual report, revenue reached nearly $7.1 million. This represented a decline of approximately 34.3% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net loss of roughly $216.2 million for the same period. This resulted in a negative net margin of approximately 3,050.4%, highlighting the intense research and development costs required to build and scale quantum processors.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x. This ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicates the company currently carries no debt on its books. The current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term bills with short-term assets, was approximately 37.4x. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was nearly negative $77.2 million. Free cash flow represents the cash a company generates after accounting for cash outflows to support operations and maintain its capital assets.
SoundHound creates voice-enabled AI software used in cars, restaurants, and smart devices. Its Houndify platform allows businesses to build natural conversational interfaces for their products. The company recently completed the acquisition of LivePerson, which helped integrate advanced customer engagement and agentic AI tools into its stack. SoundHound serves various sectors, including automotive and hospitality, through royalties and subscription contracts. Revenue is primarily derived from these long-term service contracts and the monetization of voice-enabled interactions.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $168.9 million, an increase of approximately 99.4% over previous results. The company reported a net loss of roughly $14.0 million for the fiscal year. This narrowed its negative net margin to approximately 8.3%, indicating that the business is scaling its voice AI services more efficiently than in previous periods. This top-line growth reflects the increasing demand for conversational AI across enterprise and consumer markets.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x. This indicates that the company has no total debt relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio was roughly 4.6x, measuring the company's ability to cover its short-term debts with its short-term assets. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was approximately negative $103.1 million. This reflects the significant cash burn required to scale its software platform and integrate large acquisitions like LivePerson.
Rigetti faces risks as an early-stage company with significant accumulated deficits and a continued need for external capital to fund operations. There are substantial technological hurdles to achieving quantum advantage, and failing to meet development milestones could hurt investor confidence. High customer concentration is another factor, with much of its revenue coming from a few government entities and cloud partners. Global competition from well-funded sovereign programs and giant technology firms remains intense in the quantum space.
SoundHound deals with persistent cash burn as it scales its operations to compete in the crowded AI software market. The company faces significant execution risks following the integration of LivePerson, which could impact its financial stability if synergies are not realized. Competition from larger technology companies like Amazon or Microsoft presents ongoing pricing pressure and may limit market share. There are also potential regulatory hurdles regarding the use of generative AI technologies and data privacy concerns that could impact adoption.
Neither company currently has a positive Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, so investors often look to the P/S ratio for comparison. The P/S ratio measures a stock's market value against its sales over the past twelve months.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with SoundHound AI, though neither company is a comfortable pick right now. Both are unprofitable and asking investors to bet on technologies still finding their commercial footing.
But SoundHound has something Rigetti is still working toward: a growing base of paying enterprise customers across healthcare, automotive, and restaurant industries. Revenue grew at a strong double-digit rate in the most recent quarter, the company raised its full-year outlook, and the voice AI platform is winning new enterprise customers across multiple industries.
Rigetti has made progress on its quantum hardware, and a CHIPS Act funding letter adds a layer of government validation. But revenue remains small, and the gap between its bookings momentum and actual recognized revenue is something investors need to understand before buying in.
Both stocks are speculative and carry significant risk. But SoundHound is closer to building a durable commercial business, and for a patient investor comfortable with early-stage volatility, that gives it a modest edge right now.

remained in the spotlight on Wednesday, the last session of September, as quantum computing shares traded in choppy fashion while broader American indexes edged higher on strength in semiconductors and artificial intelligence infrastructure. The full-stack quantum company has slid in recent sessions and sits well below its yearly peak, reflecting a cooling of the enthusiasm that carried the group sharply higher earlier in the cycle.
The company reported second-quarter results in August that pointed to growing demand for its quantum systems, progress on its technology roadmap and continued support from the federal government. Even so, the revenue base remains small relative to the scale of the ambitions in the field, and the stock has reacted more to sentiment about the sector than to any single quarterly update.
On the final day of the month, the market's appetite was clearly pointed toward established chip and cloud names. Alphabet rose after a stake disclosed by Berkshire Hathaway, and Micron drew attention around memory results. Speculative technology names such as Rigetti moved in a much less orderly way, with wide intraday ranges and light conviction.
Sector Background For Frontier Technology Shares
Frontier technology companies form an important slice of penny stocks, where share prices are driven by narrative as much as by financial statements. Quantum computing, small modular nuclear reactors, space launch and advanced batteries all share a common feature: the science is real, the commercial timing is uncertain, and market enthusiasm arrives in waves.
Quantum computing in particular attracted enormous retail attention after a period of dramatic share price gains. Endorsements from prominent technology executives, government funding announcements and breakthroughs in error correction each contributed to rallies. Reversals came just as quickly when expectations ran ahead of engineering progress.
That backdrop explains why quantum shares have proved so volatile. With modest revenue, heavy research spending and a long road to fault-tolerant machines, the equity story depends on confidence in roadmap execution and in the willingness of governments and enterprises to keep funding early systems.
Rigetti designs and manufactures superconducting quantum processors and builds the systems and software needed to operate them. Unlike firms that focus only on software or cloud access, the company controls the full stack, from chip fabrication in its own facility to control electronics, compilers and cloud delivery of quantum computing resources.
Its chips are built from superconducting circuits cooled to extremely low temperatures, where electrical current behaves according to quantum rules. The company has pursued a modular approach, combining smaller chips into larger systems in order to improve reliability and scale. That chiplet strategy is designed to reduce manufacturing difficulty and improve the quality of qubits.
Customers include government laboratories, universities, and enterprises exploring how quantum machines might one day solve optimization, simulation and materials science problems. The company also offers smaller on-premises systems aimed at research institutions and national programs that want hands-on access to hardware.
The company also maintains software tools and a cloud interface so that researchers can program its machines without deep hardware knowledge, lowering the barrier for new users and helping build a community around the platform.
Recent Developments And Second-Quarter Update
The August update emphasized several themes. Management highlighted growing demand for quantum systems, technical progress toward higher fidelity operation, and strategic support from the federal government. Revenue for the quarter was modest, and the company continued to report a sizable net loss, which is typical for a business in a heavy research phase.
A notable feature of the balance sheet is the substantial cash position built through earlier equity raises during the height of market enthusiasm. That liquidity gives the company a long runway to keep developing its roadmap without immediate reliance on additional financing, a point often noted when comparing quantum developers with other cash-hungry technology start-ups.
Government engagement has been a recurring source of encouragement. Federal programs seeking to identify practical paths to utility-scale quantum computers have included multiple companies in early evaluation phases, and participation is regarded as validation of technical direction, even though it does not guarantee commercial success.
Technology Roadmap And Operational Focus
The central engineering challenge for every quantum company is error correction. Qubits are fragile, and useful computation requires many physical qubits to form a smaller number of dependable logical ones. Rigetti has focused on improving two-qubit gate fidelity, which is the accuracy of the basic operation on which more complex algorithms depend.
Scaling the number of qubits while maintaining quality is the second focus. Modular architectures allow engineers to test individual chips before assembling them, improving yield. The company has described a sequence of increasingly capable systems, with each generation intended to demonstrate better fidelity and larger size.
Operational execution also involves fabrication, cryogenic systems and software tooling. Running its own foundry offers control over process improvements but requires steady capital expenditure. Maintaining cadence on chip releases, while meeting delivery commitments for customer systems, will be closely observed by the market.
Industry Developments In Quantum Computing
Across the industry, momentum has shifted toward error-corrected designs. Large technology firms have unveiled chips that demonstrate progress in suppressing errors, and start-ups have announced roadmaps stretching over several years. Each announcement affects the perceived competitive standing of all participants, including smaller public companies.
Different hardware approaches are competing. Superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms and photonics each offer distinct advantages in speed, connectivity or manufacturability. No approach has yet clearly won, and the market tends to reward whichever modality most recently posted an impressive technical result.
Government and defense interest remains a stabilizing force. National strategies for quantum technology, funding for research centers and procurement programs create a base of demand that does not rely solely on commercial enterprises. That support is particularly valuable for small companies that lack the deep resources of the largest technology groups.
Rigetti competes with technology giants such as IBM and Google, which pursue superconducting approaches with vast resources, as well as with other listed specialists such as IonQ and D-Wave, each with a different technology or business model. Private companies and university spin-offs further crowd the field.
Its differentiators include the in-house fabrication facility, the modular chip strategy, and its position as one of the few pure-play superconducting developers accessible to public market participants. Its challenge is scale: larger rivals can fund longer research cycles and absorb setbacks that would strain a smaller company.
Partnerships play a key role in bridging that gap. Collaborations with manufacturers, cloud platforms and national laboratories help spread costs, expand distribution and lend credibility. The market watches for new alliances as a signal of commercial traction.
Market Environment On The Final Day Of September
American indexes edged higher led by technology. Semiconductor and infrastructure names for artificial intelligence were firm, and Alphabet jumped after news of a stake held by Berkshire Hathaway. Micron's memory results drew attention as a gauge of demand for data center hardware. Financials were among the weaker groups of the month, and energy slipped as crude eased on reserve releases and a stalemate between Washington and Tehran.
Quantum computing stocks often behave like a high-beta extension of the technology trade, rising sharply when sentiment is buoyant and falling when traders rotate toward safer or more proven ideas. Recent sessions have seen the latter pattern, with shares of Rigetti retreating even as large-cap technology advanced.
That divergence illustrates how narrowly strength has been distributed. Companies with tangible revenue tied to artificial intelligence spending have been rewarded, while pre-commercial technology stories must rely on belief in long-term possibilities, a harder case to make in days of heavy focus on near-term earnings.
Commercial demand is the most significant uncertainty. Today's quantum computers cannot yet outperform classical machines on most practical tasks, so revenue comes mainly from research contracts, system sales to laboratories and access programs. Converting curiosity into recurring enterprise spending will require demonstrable advantages.
Technical hurdles remain formidable. Error rates, cooling requirements, wiring complexity and manufacturing consistency all limit scale. Breakthroughs are possible, but timelines have a habit of stretching, and market participants have learned to treat ambitious roadmaps with measured skepticism.
Financial discipline adds another layer. Companies in the field have raised large amounts of capital during rallies, and the way they use it, including acquisitions, facility expansion and hiring, will shape later dilution and cash needs. Transparent capital allocation is increasingly valued by market participants.
Rigetti's positioning rests on being an integrated hardware developer with its own fabrication capability and a clear modular scaling plan. That control allows faster iteration and closer coordination between chip design and system engineering, benefits that matter in a field where small improvements in materials or layout can unlock large gains.
The company also benefits from its alignment with government priorities. Quantum technology is viewed as strategically important for national security, cryptography, and scientific competitiveness, so federal agencies have shown willingness to fund domestic hardware development. Being a domestic supplier with in-house manufacturing is an advantage in that environment.
The counterweight is scale and time. The business must sustain years of research spending before mass-market utility arrives, and it must do so while rivals with deeper pockets pursue similar goals. Balancing steady progress against cash preservation is the central strategic task.
Broader Market Relevance And What Comes Next
Quantum computing has become a barometer for speculative appetite in technology. When the group rallies, it typically signals strong appetite for speculation across the market, and when it slides, it can point to a more cautious mood. The recent decline hints at a more selective environment, where evidence of execution matters more than enthusiasm.

pages.text:

Rigetti Builds Commercial Momentum With Hybrid Quantum-HPC Strategy
Rigetti Computing RGTI is increasingly positioning its superconducting quantum computing technology for integration into high-performance computing (HPC) environments. A key development is the company's expanded collaboration with Hewlett Packard Enterprise HPE and the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center ("PSC"), under which Rigetti will provide a full 9-qubit Novera quantum computing system for PSC's TangleLab test bed. The system is expected to combine Rigetti's quantum processor, refrigeration and control infrastructure with Hewlett Packard's HPC environment, allowing researchers and industry users to develop and test hybrid quantum-classical workloads. Rigetti expects the deployment in 2027. Management views the initiative as an important step toward moving its relationship with Hewlett Packard from early experimentation to commercially relevant quantum-enabled HPC solutions.
The hybrid computing opportunity is particularly relevant to Rigetti's strategy because the company believes its superconducting architecture can provide the processing speed needed to work alongside conventional CPUs and GPUs. Management cited gate speeds in the 50-60 nanosecond range and highlighted the potential for faster quantum processing to complement classical computing in workloads where quantum acceleration can reduce time to results or improve computational capabilities.
Beyond the collaboration with HPE, Rigetti is also seeing increasing interest from commercial organizations. The company delivered its first two 9-qubit systems in 2026 to commercial customers for research purposes. While these deployments do not yet represent production quantum workloads, the broader customer mix suggests that commercial engagement is beginning to develop alongside government and university demand.
With Rigetti continuing to improve the fidelity of its 108-qubit Cepheus system and pursuing a chiplet-based roadmap toward approximately 1,000 qubits, the company's strategy is increasingly centered on building the infrastructure and partnerships needed to support broader quantum adoption as the technology advances.
Quantum Computing Inc. QUBT recently signed a three-year Framework Agreement with Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Qatar to collaborate on quantum computing, quantum sensing and quantum communications initiatives. The partnership will support joint academic research, executive education programs, industry-focused projects, quantum application development and co-marketing efforts aimed at accelerating quantum technology adoption across Qatar and beyond. The companies also plan to develop practical quantum solutions for real-world challenges while helping cultivate the next generation of quantum talent and leadership.
IonQ IONQ recently announced a contract with Florida International University ("FIU") to deliver and install a Superion 256-qubit trapped-ion quantum computer on the university's campus. The agreement marks the first sale and deployment of a Superion 256 system in Florida and establishes FIU as IonQ's flagship academic partner in the state, creating a hub for quantum research, education and workforce development. The on-campus deployment is expected to provide FIU's faculty, students and regional industry partners with direct access to advanced quantum computing capabilities, while FIU's engagement with federal agencies could support research initiatives spanning sensing, cryptography, commercialization and workforce development.
The partnership strengthens IonQ's presence in the academic quantum ecosystem and expands physical access to its hardware, potentially supporting broader adoption and talent development in the region.

The current ratio stands at roughly 1.8x, suggesting the ability to pay short-term obligations with current assets. Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was negative $46.3 million. This negative figure highlights that the company is currently consuming cash to fund its growth and acquisition initiatives.
Rigetti Computing builds full-stack quantum computers, including superconducting processors and cloud services. Its applications span drug discovery and logistics for government, academic, and commercial clients. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company noted that U.S. government entities accounted for nearly 90.2% of its total revenue. It maintains distribution partnerships with cloud giants Amazon (AMZN -0.05%) and Microsoft (MSFT +1.48%). A major collaboration with Quanta also focuses on developing quantum computing components.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $7.1 million, which is a decline of roughly 34.3% from the prior year. The company reported a net loss of approximately $216.2 million, which widened from a $201.0 million net loss in 2024. These figures reflect the early-stage nature of the quantum computing industry, where research and development costs far exceed current sales. The net margin of approximately negative 3,050.4% highlights the significant gap between the company's early revenue and its operational spending.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x, indicating that the firm has no total debt relative to its equity. The current ratio was approximately 37.4x, which suggests a very high level of liquidity to meet short-term liabilities. Free cash flow, calculating cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was negative $77.2 million. This negative cash flow indicates the high capital intensity required to build and maintain sophisticated quantum hardware and fabrication facilities.
BigBear.ai faces significant risks, particularly its heavy reliance on government and public sector customers whose contracts can be terminated for convenience. The company is also managing a material class action lawsuit related to previous accounting errors and mandatory financial statement restatements. Integration of its artificial intelligence technologies also poses operational hurdles. Furthermore, the company depends on third-party cloud infrastructure and must compete with massive, well-capitalized defense firms that possess larger research budgets.
Rigetti Computing faces substantial technical risks as it attempts to achieve quantum advantage, a goal with no guarantee of success. The company is dealing with a class action lawsuit and a history of significant net losses and accumulated deficits. It is highly dependent on a small number of government customers and public cloud providers such as Amazon and Microsoft. Additionally, the business requires heavy research and development spending for its fabrication facility upgrades and intellectual property protection.
BigBear.ai appears cheaper based on its P/S ratio, which compares market capitalization to sales over the past twelve months.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with BigBear.ai. Both companies are early-stage, unprofitable, and asking investors to bet on technologies that are still proving themselves, so this is not a comfortable pick either way.
That said, BigBear.ai has something Rigetti is still working toward: revenue from customers that are difficult to displace. Its AI-powered decision intelligence platform is embedded in national security workflows, and the backlog keeps growing. The path to profitability is long, but the direction is encouraging.
Rigetti is one of the few companies that has actually built and deployed quantum computing hardware at a scale that serious researchers are paying to access. A CHIPS Act funding letter of intent adds a layer of government validation. But revenue remains tiny, and the gap between bookings momentum and actual recognized revenue is something investors need to understand before buying in. Quantum computing's commercial moment is getting closer, but it has not fully arrived yet.
If I'm choosing between two speculative early-stage companies, I want to own the one already generating revenue from customers that are hard to walk away from. That's the more grounded starting point for a patient investor.

pages.title: Cerebras Systems vs. Rigetti Computing: Is an AI or Quantum Computing Stock the Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool

▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
The computing world is at a crossroads where current AI leaders meet the next generation of processors. Investors are now weighing whether Cerebras Systems (CBRS +9.09%) or Rigetti Computing (RGTI -0.66%) is the better buy today.
Cerebras focuses on massive chips designed to dominate AI training and inference tasks. Rigetti is building superconducting quantum computers that could eventually solve problems today's machines cannot touch. Comparing them requires weighing current revenue against long-term scientific potential.
Cerebras is carving out a unique niche among semiconductor stocks by focusing on the physical scale of its processors. Its Wafer-Scale Engine is the largest chip ever produced, designed specifically to accelerate the complex workloads required for medical research, energy modeling, and agentic AI.
In FY 2025, revenue reached about $510 million, representing growth of approximately 76% over the previous year. This rapid expansion helped the company achieve a net income of close to $238 million, indicating a significant improvement from its prior loss-making periods.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was negative 0.5x, which means total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The company maintains what is known as the current ratio of roughly 2.1x, a metric that measures the ability to cover short-term debts with current assets. Free cash flow was approximately negative $393 million, showing the cash used after accounting for necessary capital investments.
Rigetti develops superconducting quantum processors and provides access to its systems through its cloud-based platform. The company works with major partners like Amazon.com Inc (AMZN -0.05%) and Microsoft Corp (MSFT +1.48%) while also serving government agencies like NASA and the Department of Energy.
In FY 2025, revenue reached roughly $7.1 million, which was a decrease of around 34% compared to the prior fiscal year. The company reported a net loss of approximately $216 million for the period as it continued to invest heavily in research and development.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x, indicating the firm carries virtually no debt relative to its equity. The current ratio of nearly 37.4x suggests a very high level of liquidity to fund its ongoing technological roadmaps. Free cash flow was approximately negative $77.2 million, which is the cash a company generates after subtracting capital expenditures.
Cerebras faces intense competition from established chip giants and must navigate the high costs associated with proprietary manufacturing processes. The business also deals with risks regarding its dependence on the continued rapid growth of the AI market to sustain its high valuation.
Rigetti faces significant risks regarding its financial viability, given its history of operating losses and the high capital intensity of quantum hardware. It also faces a concentrated customer base and fierce competition from well-funded rivals like Alphabet Inc (GOOG +1.02%) and International Business Machines (IBM -0.48%) that are also racing to achieve quantum advantage.
Cerebras appears more reasonably valued on a Forward P/E basis, while Rigetti carries a much higher P/S ratio due to its early-stage revenue levels.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
These are two exciting companies into two of the possibly most impactful tech sectors we may see in our lifetimes.
Cerebras has a strong niche in the AI explosion and should see incredible growth in the coming years. Cerebras has transformative partnerships with OpenAI and Amazon's AWS. Much of Cerebras's projected growth relies on the AI inference market growing from $66 billion last year to $292 billion by 2029. That's a huge potential market. Based partly on projections like that, Wall Street analyst consensus figures indicate Cerebras producing about $888 million in sales in fiscal 2026, exploding to about $3 billion in 2027 and $7.5 billion in 2028. The same estimates indicate Cerebras will move to healthy profitability as soon as 2028.
Rigetti, meanwhile, seems more speculative. After all, the business had just $7 million in revenue last year. The company recently received a potential award of up to $100 million over three years to accelerate superconducting quantum computing R&D and address key technical challenges in scaling and advancing its systems. The deal, in which the federal government would also take equity in the business, would allow Rigetti to tackle key scaling bottlenecks associated with multichip architectures more rapidly. It would also enable management to accelerate multiple generations of superconducting quantum processors and associated control electronics at Fab-1, its dedicated quantum device manufacturing facility.
In short, it's a transformative deal too.
The choice here, then, is between two rather speculative stocks. Rigetti is alluring, but at the moment its P/S ratio is astonishingly high, even considering revenue projections out through the decade, which aren't seen exceeding $100 million.
That leaves Cerebras as the choice, given its existing business base and projections of rapid AI growth.

Rigetti Computing (RGTI -0.66%) looks exciting on the surface: There's government money, cutting‑edge hardware, and big language about utility‑scale quantum computers. But when you dig into the company's own numbers and plans, it looks like the stock could easily turn into a trap rather than the bargain it appears to be. Here are three reasons.\
No. 1: A small business with very ambitious promises
Rigetti's 2026 news releases make it clear the company is still a very small business trying to build a very big future. For the first quarter of 2026, total revenue was just $4.4 million, with an operating loss of $26 million and an adjusted net loss of $14.7 million. And the second quarter brought $5.1 million of revenue against a $28.1 million operating loss and an adjusted net loss of $16 million.
Image source: Getty Images.
The company ended the second quarter with $541.3 million of cash and investments and no debt, which sounds comforting. But when you compare that cash pile and revenue to the size of the losses and the scale of the road map management keeps talking about, you are reminded that this is still a pre‑profit, high‑burn story.
$5.1BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
On the technology side, Rigetti is doing interesting things. Its Cepheus‑1‑108Q chip validates a chiplet‑based architecture and is now available through its cloud, but those milestones have not yet turned into a business that can stand on its own cash flows, as you can see from this year's numbers.
If you buy the stock because the government and big partners are interested, without matching that against how small the current business is, it is easy to treat a speculative research platform like a mature company or a hype ticker.
No. 2: Government funding is helpful, but not as bullish as you think
This month, Rigetti signed a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100 million in CHIPS Act funding to accelerate research and development of superconducting quantum computing.
The program provides funds for three big projects: miniaturizing readout electronics, hugely expanding cryogenic capacity with a new cryostat design, and developing fabrication for high‑connectivity chips -- all of which are important if you care about scaling up quantum machines.
However, the details matter. The Commerce Department made $43.9 million available shortly after the award date, but the remaining $56.1 million is split into two tranches contingent on Rigetti meeting specific technical and milestone criteria. And the government retains the right to claw back funds if the company fails to perform or materially breaches the agreement.
On top of that, Rigetti agreed to issue 7,739,938 shares of common stock to the department at an implied price of $12.92 per share, giving the government a minority equity stake and diluting existing shareholders.
In other words, the CHIPS award isn't free money. It comes with milestones and dilution, and if quantum projects take longer than expected, that funding could become a burden.
No. 3: Long timelines and execution risk
Management seems very open about the fact that its road map is measured in years, not quarters. In its recent materials and earnings call, the company described the government program as a three‑year effort aimed at pushing toward utility‑scale quantum computing, while also noting that delivery of key systems tied to these programs is not expected until 2027.
Later on in the company's earnings call, management said customers are giving strong feedback on its 108-qubit system, calling it reliable, consistent, and easy to use. But it acknowledged that the quantum advantage is still a ways out before it can support practical workloads.
I'm cynical here because Rigetti has been volatile over the last couple of years, and a lot of the stock's momentum has come from bullish announcements. I'd rather see real progress on its road map and from management before buying shares. If those milestones slip or better-funded rivals pull ahead, investors could be left waiting years for the commercial traction the story promises.

RGTI vs QUBT: Which Quantum Computing Stock Has More Upside Potential?
The quantum computing race is no longer just about who can build the most powerful machine. It is increasingly becoming a contest between companies pursuing different paths to commercial adoption while convincing investors they can turn breakthrough technology into sustainable businesses.
That contrast was on full display during the latest earnings season as Rigetti Computing RGTI and Quantum Computing Inc. QUBT outlined sharply different strategies for scaling their businesses. Rigetti doubled down on its superconducting quantum computing roadmap, highlighting progress on its 108-qubit Cepheus-1 system, a modular chiplet architecture aimed at 1,000-qubit systems and growing government-backed initiatives. Meanwhile, QUBT leaned into its room-temperature photonic platform, expanding through acquisitions, semiconductor manufacturing and AI-focused photonics products designed to generate commercial revenue alongside its long-term quantum ambitions.
Both companies reported second-quarter revenues above $5 million, but the drivers behind those results looked very different. Rigetti's 185% revenue jump was fueled by quantum hardware deployments, while QUBT's 9,000% surge reflected contributions from its rapidly expanding photonics and semiconductor businesses. With both stocks competing for investor attention in one of the market's fastest-evolving industries, the bigger question is which execution strategy appears stronger based on their latest updates.
Let's get into more detail.
Rigetti's second-quarter results reinforced an execution-driven investment case as revenues jumped 185% year over year to $5.1 million, fueled by on-premises Novera QPU sales, while gross margin expanded to 43% from 31% a year ago.
Beyond the financials, the company continued advancing its 108-qubit Cepheus-1 platform, reaffirmed its chiplet-based roadmap toward roughly 1,000 qubits over the next three years, strengthened its government ties through a U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for up to $100 million in potential CHIPS Act funding and ended the quarter with $541.3 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments and no debt.
Rigetti's biggest challenge remains converting technical milestones into durable commercial scale. Although revenues grew sharply, quarterly sales remain relatively modest at $5.1 million, while operating expenses climbed to $30.3 million as the company continued investing heavily in R&D, chip design, fabrication and refrigeration infrastructure to support higher-qubit systems.
At the same time, management still needs to deliver meaningful improvements in Cepheus-1's gate fidelity and coherence times before progressing toward its 1,000-qubit ambitions, while the proposed CHIPS Act funding remains contingent on a definitive agreement and customary approvals.
Quantum Computing's second quarter highlighted a broader commercialization strategy that extends beyond quantum computing alone. Revenues surged to $5.6 million from just $61,000 a year ago, with contributions from government, commercial and educational customers across its photonics portfolio.
The company accelerated its expansion through the acquisitions of NHanced Semiconductors, Luminar Semiconductor and NuCrypt, strengthening its advanced packaging and semiconductor manufacturing capabilities while launching its Fab 2 initiative.
Commercial traction also improved with the rollout of the NeuraWave photonic AI platform, the installation of a DIRAC-3 optimization system at a global consulting firm, a multi-unit NeuraWave framework agreement with Planck Dynamics and a contract backlog that reached $42.5 million, backed by a cash and investment position of roughly $1.3 billion.
QUBT's rapid expansion also brings meaningful execution risks as the company integrates multiple acquisitions while scaling manufacturing and commercialization simultaneously. Operating expenses more than doubled to $21.8 million, due to higher R&D spending, personnel costs, sales and marketing investments and acquisition-related expenses.
The company remains heavily dependent on government-funded work, with management indicating that roughly 70%-80% of current business comes from government subcontracting, while contract timing remains lumpy and backlog is expected to be recognized over 12 to 18 months rather than translating into immediate revenue.
In addition, management is evaluating another $50-$100 million of potential investment to enhance NHanced's manufacturing capabilities, adding another layer of capital deployment and integration complexity.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for RGTI's 2026 bottom line is pegged at a loss of 19 cents per share, implying a 70.3% improvement over the 2025 reported figure.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for QUBT's 2026 bottom line is pegged at a loss of 19 cents per share, implying a 72.7% decline over the 2025 reported loss.
Based on short-term price targets offered by six analysts, the average price target for QUBT represents an increase of 103.8% from the last closing price of $9.16.
Based on short-term price targets offered by 11 analysts, the average price target for RGTI represents an increase of 79.1% from the last closing price of $16.50.
Final Take: RGTI or QUBT?
The latest earnings season highlighted two very different execution stories. QUBT paired revenue growth with expanding commercial traction through acquisitions, a growing photonics business, a $42.5 million backlog and a sizeable $1.3 billion cash position, while Rigetti's quarter centered on advancing its superconducting roadmap, government partnerships and long-term technology milestones. Analyst sentiment also reflects a wider upside outlook for QUBT, with its average price target implying 103.8% upside from recent levels compared with 79.1% for Rigetti.
The two stocks entered the next phase with different outlooks. QUBT currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), reflecting a more balanced near-term earnings outlook, while Rigetti carries a Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), indicating weaker earnings expectations. Although QUBT appears better positioned from a commercialization and analyst-sentiment standpoint, both companies remain high-risk plays in an emerging industry where execution, customer adoption and technology milestones will likely remain the key factors to watch.

pages.title: IonQ vs. Rigetti Computing: Which Pure-Play Quantum Stock Actually Has the Technology Edge? | The Motley Fool
pages.text:
▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI -0.66%) are taking entirely different technological routes in their efforts to build useful quantum computers.
IonQ uses trapped-ion technology, where individual charged atoms held in place by precise electromagnetic fields serve as qubits, the basic units of information in any quantum computer. Rigetti Computing uses superconducting qubits, which are tiny electrical circuits cooled to extremely low temperatures.
Image source: Getty Images.
IonQ has demonstrated more than 99.99% fidelity, or accuracy, for 2-qubit gates (operations performed on 2 qubits at the same time). Rigetti Computing has reported roughly 99.1% median 2-qubit fidelity on its 108-qubit Cepheus system. Hence, its typical 2-qubit operation succeeds about 99.1% of the time.
While IonQ may appear to be the obvious technology winner, these figures are not directly comparable. IonQ's 99.99% result came from testing a particular 2-qubit operation, rather than measuring the overall performance of a large commercial quantum computer. A more comparable measure comes from IonQ's Forte systems, which have reported a median 2-qubit fidelity of 99.3% to 99.5%. Hence, although IonQ's qubits still appear to perform operations more accurately than Rigetti Computing's, the gap in accuracy between them is much smaller.
That narrower accuracy gap could prove crucial when quantum calculations become more complex. Using the more comparable figures above, 99.5% fidelity implies an error rate of roughly 0.5%, compared with about 0.9% at 99.1%. Hence, Rigetti Computing's error rate is roughly 1.8 times as high in this comparison.
$17BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
IonQ also has an advantage in how its qubits communicate. The company's trapped-ion systems offer all-to-all connectivity, meaning any qubit can directly interact with another qubit in the system.
Quantum computers with more limited connectivity may need additional operations, known as SWAP gates, to move quantum information between qubits that cannot directly interact. These extra operations can introduce more errors.
IonQ's connectivity can therefore reduce the number of operations needed for some quantum calculations. This can partly offset IonQ's slower quantum gates, which are the basic operations performed on qubits. In one published comparison, IonQ's Forte systems took about 950 microseconds for a 2-qubit gate, while Rigetti Computing's 108-qubit Cepheus system performed such gates in about 60 nanoseconds.
IonQ also needs to prove that the advantages of trapped-ion technology persist as its quantum computers become larger. The company's next-generation Superion 256 platform is designed around 256 qubits. IonQ has already manufactured 256-qubit Superion processor chips at SkyWater, the semiconductor foundry it acquired in July. The company has also successfully trapped ions on prototype versions of the system. However, these systems are not yet being delivered to customers; commercial deliveries are expected to begin in 2027.
In short, the Superion 256 is an important milestone, but the real test for IonQ will be whether its hardware can maintain high accuracy and connectivity as the number of qubits increases.
IonQ has also made progress in quantum error correction, which combines multiple physical qubits to create more reliable logical qubits. In one experiment, the company used 18 physical qubits to encode 4 logical qubits. Some of those logical qubits preserved quantum information for about as long as, or slightly longer than, the individual physical qubits. Researchers call this breakeven performance. This is still far from a fault-tolerant quantum computer, but it shows that IonQ has begun demonstrating its error-correction approach on actual hardware rather than only through simulations.
DARPA -- the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency -- has also advanced IonQ to Stage B of its Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. At this stage, the agency is evaluating the company's development plan, technical risks, and the prototypes needed to reduce those risks.
Rigetti Computing's quantum computing technology
Rigetti's much faster quantum computing operations could give it a major advantage if it can improve accuracy while building larger systems.
$5.1BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
The company has already made progress on the scale front. Its 108-qubit Cepheus system combines 12 interconnected 9-qubit chiplets into a 108-qubit processor. Chiplets are smaller processor blocks that can be connected to build larger systems. Rigetti Computing says this approach can help it increase the qubit counts of its quantum computers while avoiding the manufacturing complexities of building increasingly large chips.
However, Rigetti Computing has reported a median 2-qubit fidelity of 99.8% on its 9-qubit system and 99.6% on its 36-qubit system. The figure fell to roughly 99.1% on the 108-qubit Cepheus system. So while it has demonstrated that it can build larger quantum computers, maintaining accuracy as qubit count increases remains a challenge.
Management has set a goal of developing a system with roughly 1,000 qubits, 99.9% 2-qubit fidelity, and 2-qubit operations that take less than 50 nanoseconds, and given itself a timeline of approximately three years. If Rigetti Computing can build a single quantum computer that achieves all of those milestones, its combination of speed, accuracy, and scale could significantly narrow the gap between its tech and IonQ's.
Which company has the technology edge?
I think IonQ has the technology edge today. The company has moved beyond building more physical qubits to demonstrating error correction on actual hardware.
However, its lead is not secure. The Superion 256 is still in the prototype stage. IonQ still needs to prove that its accuracy and connectivity can hold up as its systems become much larger. Rigetti Computing could narrow the gap if it improves accuracy while preserving its existing advantages in speed and scalability.

Rigetti Computing vs. SoundHound AI: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Is the future of computing quantum or conversational? Investors deciding between Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) and SoundHound AI (NASDAQ:SOUN) must choose which high-growth technology offers the better long-term potential for their portfolios.
Rigetti is a pioneer in building superconducting quantum computers, while SoundHound provides voice-enabled artificial intelligence software for diverse industries. They are being compared because both represent small-cap bets on the next generation of artificial intelligence, though they operate at opposite ends of the hardware and software spectrum.
Rigetti sells superconducting quantum processors and cloud-based quantum services to research and commercial clients. The company remains a pioneer among tech stocks, particularly within the nascent quantum hardware industry. It serves customers through its Quantum Cloud Services platform, targeting complex problems in fields like climate simulation and drug discovery. Major partners include Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), which provide broad cloud access to its hardware. Significant government clients like DARPA also utilize its technology, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.
In FY 2025, according to its latest annual report, revenue reached nearly $7.1 million. This represented a decline of approximately 34.3% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net loss of roughly $216.2 million for the same period. This resulted in a negative net margin of approximately 3,050.4%, highlighting the intense research and development costs required to build and scale quantum processors.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x. This ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicates the company currently carries no debt on its books. The current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term bills with short-term assets, was approximately 37.4x. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was nearly negative $77.2 million. Free cash flow represents the cash a company generates after accounting for cash outflows to support operations and maintain its capital assets.
SoundHound creates voice-enabled AI software used in cars, restaurants, and smart devices. Its Houndify platform allows businesses to build natural conversational interfaces for their products. The company recently completed the acquisition of LivePerson, which helped integrate advanced customer engagement and agentic AI tools into its stack. SoundHound serves various sectors, including automotive and hospitality, through royalties and subscription contracts. Revenue is primarily derived from these long-term service contracts and the monetization of voice-enabled interactions.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $168.9 million, an increase of approximately 99.4% over previous results. The company reported a net loss of roughly $14.0 million for the fiscal year. This narrowed its negative net margin to approximately 8.3%, indicating that the business is scaling its voice AI services more efficiently than in previous periods. This top-line growth reflects the increasing demand for conversational AI across enterprise and consumer markets.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x. This indicates that the company has no total debt relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio was roughly 4.6x, measuring the company's ability to cover its short-term debts with its short-term assets. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was approximately negative $103.1 million. This reflects the significant cash burn required to scale its software platform and integrate large acquisitions like LivePerson.
Rigetti faces risks as an early-stage company with significant accumulated deficits and a continued need for external capital to fund operations. There are substantial technological hurdles to achieving quantum advantage, and failing to meet development milestones could hurt investor confidence. High customer concentration is another factor, with much of its revenue coming from a few government entities and cloud partners. Global competition from well-funded sovereign programs and giant technology firms remains intense in the quantum space.
SoundHound deals with persistent cash burn as it scales its operations to compete in the crowded AI software market. The company faces significant execution risks following the integration of LivePerson, which could impact its financial stability if synergies are not realized. Competition from larger technology companies like Amazon or Microsoft presents ongoing pricing pressure and may limit market share. There are also potential regulatory hurdles regarding the use of generative AI technologies and data privacy concerns that could impact adoption.
Neither company currently has a positive Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, so investors often look to the P/S ratio for comparison. The P/S ratio measures a stock's market value against its sales over the past twelve months.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with SoundHound AI, though neither company is a comfortable pick right now. Both are unprofitable and asking investors to bet on technologies still finding their commercial footing.
But SoundHound has something Rigetti is still working toward: a growing base of paying enterprise customers across healthcare, automotive, and restaurant industries. Revenue grew at a strong double-digit rate in the most recent quarter, the company raised its full-year outlook, and the voice AI platform is winning new enterprise customers across multiple industries.
Rigetti has made progress on its quantum hardware, and a CHIPS Act funding letter adds a layer of government validation. But revenue remains small, and the gap between its bookings momentum and actual recognized revenue is something investors need to understand before buying in.
Both stocks are speculative and carry significant risk. But SoundHound is closer to building a durable commercial business, and for a patient investor comfortable with early-stage volatility, that gives it a modest edge right now.
